overview: Barramundi Limited is a NZX Main Board-listed closed-end investment company (inception 26 October 2006) that gives New Zealand investors a single, tax-efficient (PIE) vehicle for a concentrated portfolio of growing Australian-listed and unlisted companies. Barramundi has no employees or operating business of its own: its board outsources all investment decisions to external manager Fisher Funds Management Limited, which applies a proprietary 'STEEPP' stock-selection process to build a portfolio of roughly 25-35 mid/large-cap Australian growth names (current top holdings include WiseTech, Macquarie Group, Xero, BHP Group and CSL). It is not a growth compounder in the operating-company sense; it is a wrapper whose investor return equals the underlying Australian equity return, minus manager fees, plus or minus any change in the market's discount/premium to net asset value (NAV).

business_model.summary: Barramundi earns no 'revenue' in the operating sense — its statement of comprehensive income comprises dividend and interest income from the portfolio (~$4-6m p.a.) plus (usually much larger and far more volatile) unrealised and realised gains/losses on the Australian equity portfolio and associated NZD/AUD currency hedges. FY2025 net profit was $7.9m (comprising a $12.5m total loss/income line net of a $8.5m fair-value gain, $4.9m dividend/interest income, and $4.0m operating expenses); H1 FY2026 (six months to 31-Dec-2025) swung to a $15.4m net LOSS as the portfolio's fair value fell $17.4m. Barramundi is structured as a Portfolio Investment Entity (PIE) for NZ tax purposes, meaning most capital gains on ASX-listed holdings are tax-exempt to the company, and shareholders' distributions carry favourable PIE tax treatment relative to direct offshore share ownership.

revenue_streams.name: Dividend income from Australian equity portfolio
revenue_streams.trend: stable, modest (~2% yield on assets); this is the only genuinely recurring 'earnings' stream

revenue_streams.name: Net change in fair value of investments (capital gains/losses, realised + unrealised)
revenue_streams.trend: highly volatile and market-driven — FY2024 +$28.9m, FY2025 +$7.8m, H1 FY2026 -$17.4m — this is the dominant, non-recurring swing factor in reported profit, not a business revenue stream

business_model.customer_type: NZ retail and wealth-adviser shareholders seeking diversified, PIE-tax-efficient exposure to Australian growth equities without direct ASX brokerage/FX/tax complexity; no institutional or wholesale 'customer' base in the operating-company sense
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% market risk concentrated in Australia (single operating segment: 'Australian financial investment'); reporting currency NZD but ~91% of assets are AUD-denominated Australian-listed equities, actively hedged back toward NZD via forward FX contracts at the Manager's discretion (not fully or permanently hedged, so currency risk fluctuates through time)

main_competitors: Australian Foundation Investment Company (AFIC/AFI.NZ dual-listed peer LIC)
Fisher Funds' own open-ended Australian/international funds
ASX 200 / S&P/ASX Small Ords index ETFs (e.g., hedged Australian equity ETFs available to NZ investors)
Other NZX-listed closed-end funds (e.g., Marlin Global — also Fisher Funds-managed, international equities sister fund)
Direct ASX share ownership via NZ brokers (FX/tax/diversification trade-off alternative)
competitive_position.market_position: Small-cap NZX-listed vehicle; market capitalisation has fallen sharply, roughly NZ$165-225m through 2026 versus $240m+ shareholders' equity at 30-Jun-2025, reflecting both a falling NAV and a widening discount. Sub-scale relative to global peers, which caps secondary-market liquidity and limits the fund's ability to attract larger wholesale/KiwiSaver allocations.

moat_factors.description: As a Portfolio Investment Entity, most ASX capital gains are tax-exempt to Barramundi and distributions receive favourable PIE tax treatment for NZ resident shareholders versus direct offshore share ownership (which is typically subject to the Fair Dividend Rate regime) — a genuine structural advantage that is hard for a retail investor to replicate independently.

moat_factors.factor: Manager fee alignment / performance-fee downside protection
moat_factors.description: The base management fee mechanically steps down (0.1% per 1% of underperformance versus the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index, floor 0.75%) when the Manager underperforms — as it did in H1 FY2026, when the fee was cut from 1.25% to 0.75% of gross asset value — partially cushioning shareholders during weak periods, unlike most externally managed funds where the base fee is fixed regardless of performance.

Fisher Funds has managed the fund since 2006 using a documented 'STEEPP' (Strength of business, Track record, Earnings history, Earnings growth forecast, People/management, Price/valuation) process; longevity provides some governance continuity but has not translated into consistent benchmark outperformance in recent years.

A ~25-35 stock concentrated portfolio theoretically allows genuine active-management alpha versus a passive index, but recent multi-year results show this concentration has been a source of underperformance (AI/tech and classified-advertising drawdowns) rather than outperformance.

weaknesses: Persistent, and in 2026 sharply widening, share price discount to NAV (around 11-13% by late July 2026, versus the Board's 6% share-buyback trigger threshold) — the market structurally does not value the underlying assets at 100 cents in the dollar

Recent manager underperformance versus benchmark: FY2025 adjusted NAV return +3.9% versus the S&P/ASX 200 (70% hedged) benchmark +13.5%; H1 FY2026 adjusted NAV return -6.6% versus benchmark +5.6% — a very large, two-period relative shortfall

8%-p.a. quarterly distribution policy (2% of average NAV per quarter) is materially higher than the portfolio's underlying dividend yield, so in years of weak capital performance the distribution is effectively a return of shareholders' own capital, eroding the NAV base per share over time

Warrant issuance programme is a recurring, structurally dilutive feature: warrants are issued free to existing shareholders (1-for-4 in Aug-2025) and if exercised below prevailing NAV per share, dilute NAV for non-participating or already-diluted holders; if unexercised (as increasingly likely given the Aug-2025 warrants carry a $0.70 strike against an NAV that has fallen to ~$0.53-0.54 by mid-2026) they simply lapse, but the overhang and periodic capital-raising cycle is a permanent feature investors must underwrite
Sub-scale fund size limits secondary-market liquidity, which can itself widen the discount in periods of selling pressure (a negative feedback loop)
Single-country, single-currency-block concentration (100% Australia) offers no diversification benefit versus a global or NZ-only alternative

growth_drivers: Potential discount narrowing: the Company operates an active share buyback programme that is triggered whenever the share price discount to last-published NAV (adjusted for index moves) exceeds 6% — if executed at scale, buybacks are NAV-accretive per remaining share and can help close the gap that has recently widened to 11-13%

Portfolio exposure to structural Australian/ASX growth and quality names (WiseTech, Xero, CSL, Macquarie Group, BHP) gives shareholders participation in secular themes (software, healthcare/plasma therapeutics, resources) without direct ASX account administration

Manager's opportunistic portfolio tilts, e.g. adding BHP and Rio Tinto in H1 FY2026 to capture commodity price strength, and continued conviction in technology holdings (WiseTech, Xero) despite recent AI-related derating, could support a recovery in relative performance if executed well

Fee step-down mechanism partially self-corrects during underperformance (management fee cut to 0.75% in H1 FY2026), somewhat cushioning shareholder returns and creating an incentive for the Manager to restore outperformance to earn back the higher fee and any performance fee
Dividend reinvestment plan (3% discount to 5-day VWAP) provides a modest structural NAV-accretion mechanic for participating shareholders and steady demand for newly issued shares

business.description: FY2025 adjusted NAV return of +3.9% versus benchmark +13.5%, followed by a -6.6% adjusted NAV return in H1 FY2026 versus benchmark +5.6%, is a material, multi-period shortfall; the Chair has publicly acknowledged 'a tough period' driven by weak stock-specific results in technology and classified-advertising holdings amid AI-related investor concerns.

A ~25-35 stock portfolio with historically no single holding above ~10% of total assets (CSL was 7-11% in recent years) still means individual company-specific shocks can meaningfully move NAV, as seen in H1 FY2026's $17.4m portfolio loss.

Market capitalisation in the NZ$150-230m range and thin secondary-market trading can amplify discount volatility and make it harder for larger investors to build or exit positions without moving the price.

Performance is dependent on Fisher Funds' portfolio team (Senior Portfolio Manager Robbie Urquhart, CIO Frank Jasper) and the STEEPP process continuing to be applied effectively; any departure of key personnel or change of manager would be a governance event for shareholders to assess.

financial.description: ~91% of assets are AUD-denominated Australian equities; NZ investors' NZD-denominated returns are exposed to AUD/NZD movements. The Manager partially and variably hedges via forward FX contracts (H1 FY2026 saw a $12.8m loss on forward FX contracts, on top of a $17.9m loss on the underlying Australian investments), so hedging can itself be a source of volatility rather than pure risk reduction.

financial.risk: Distribution exceeding earned return erodes capital
financial.description: The 8% p.a. (2% per quarter of average NAV) distribution policy is not tied to actual portfolio income or total return; in periods where the adjusted NAV return is below 8% (as in FY2025 at +3.9% and clearly in H1 FY2026 at -6.6%), the distribution is substantially a return of shareholders' own capital, which mechanically lowers the NAV base per share and can create a self-reinforcing capital-shrinkage dynamic if sustained.

Periodic 1-for-4 warrant issues (most recently Aug-2025, 85.2m warrants, exercise price $0.70, exercise date 7-Aug-2026) are dilutive to non-participating shareholders if exercised below NAV, and create a recurring capital-structure event every 1-2 years that shareholders must track; conversely, warrants well out-of-the-money (as the Aug-2025 tranche now is, given NAV has fallen from ~$0.71 at issue to ~$0.53-0.54 by mid-2026) are likely to lapse, denying the Company the expected capital raise.

regulatory.description: Barramundi's structural tax efficiency for NZ shareholders depends on continued PIE and imputation/FDR settings under NZ tax law; any adverse legislative change to PIE taxation would reduce the vehicle's relative attractiveness.

As an FMC Reporting Entity under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 and NZX Main Board listed issuer, Barramundi bears ongoing compliance, audit, custody, and climate-reporting (XRB climate statement) costs that scale poorly for a sub-scale fund.

macro.description: As a ~90%+ invested Australian equity vehicle, NAV moves essentially one-for-one (before currency and stock-selection effects) with the ASX/S&P ASX 200, making the stock highly cyclical and directly exposed to any Australian or global equity market downturn.

H1 FY2026 underperformance was explicitly attributed in part to 'AI-related investor concerns' hitting information technology and classified-advertising holdings; continued volatility in AI-driven technology valuations is a live risk given the portfolio's meaningful technology weighting (WiseTech, Xero).
Recent additions of BHP and Rio Tinto increase the portfolio's sensitivity to iron ore and broader commodity price cycles, a new but currently modest exposure.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian equities (S&P/ASX 200) have generally been resilient through 2025-2026, but Barramundi's own portfolio has lagged the benchmark materially over the most recent 12-18 months, so the fund's fortunes are currently more a function of manager stock selection than of the broad Australian equity market outlook.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — as a ~90%+ invested single-country equity closed-end fund, both NAV and the traded share price (further amplified by discount/premium swings) are directly cyclical with the Australian sharemarket and with the AUD/NZD exchange rate.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity (no company borrowings currently outstanding, no bond-like liabilities), but the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index sets both the management-fee reduction threshold and the performance-fee hurdle (Bank Bill Index + 7%), so relative NZ interest-rate levels affect the fee economics between Barramundi and Fisher Funds.
key_input_costs: Management fees paid to Fisher Funds (1.25% of gross asset value, stepping down to a 0.75% floor on underperformance)
Potential performance fees (10% of excess return over the hurdle, capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV, subject to high-water mark)
Custody, audit, NZX and administration costs

recent_developments.event: Discount to NAV widened sharply: as at 22-Jul-2026 undiluted NAV was $0.5312 with the shares trading at $0.4710 (an 11% discount), widening further to a 13% discount by 29-Jul-2026 (NAV $0.5442, share price $0.4750) — well above the Company's 6% share-buyback trigger threshold, prompting active buyback purchases.

Reported a net loss after tax of $15.4m for the six months to 31-Dec-2025 (versus a $8.9m profit in the pcp), with adjusted NAV return of -6.6% versus the benchmark's +5.6% — Chair Andy Coupe acknowledged 'a tough period' driven by weak results in technology and classified-advertising holdings amid AI-related investor concerns; management fee stepped down from 1.25% to 0.75% of gross asset value due to the 7.4-percentage-point underperformance versus the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index.
Manager added BHP Group and Rio Tinto to the portfolio to capture commodity price strength, a shift from the fund's traditional technology/healthcare/financials tilt.

Issued 85,179,108 new warrants (1-for-4 to eligible shareholders on record 6-Aug-2025), listed on NZX as BRMWI, exercise price $0.70 (adjusted down for dividends declared), exercise date 7-Aug-2026 — this warrant tranche is now deeply out-of-the-money given NAV has fallen to roughly $0.53-0.54, making significant exercise/capital-raising unlikely.

Reported FY2025 (year to 30-Jun-2025) net profit after tax of $7.9m and an adjusted NAV return of +3.9%, versus the S&P/ASX 200 (70% hedged) benchmark return of +13.5% — a large relative shortfall; NAV per share fell from $0.76 (Jun-2024, adjusted) to a reported $0.71 (undiluted NAV per financial statements) at 30-Jun-2025; total shareholder return for the year was +9.9%.
50,119,078 warrants (from the Oct-2023 tranche) were exercised at $0.63/warrant, raising a net $31.5m for the Company; the remaining 19,365,132 warrants from that tranche lapsed unexercised.

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Interim Report (16-Feb-2026) and FY2025 Annual Report (18-Aug-2025)

items.target: 2% of average NAV per quarter (~8% p.a.)
items.notes: Not formal 'guidance' in the operating-company sense but a standing Board policy; because this rate is not tied to actual earned NAV return, in periods of sub-8% total return (as in FY2025 at +3.9% and H1 FY2026 at -6.6%) the distribution is materially a return of shareholder capital, not distributed profit. Board declared 1.28 cents per share on 16-Feb-2026, record date 5-Mar-2026, payment 27-Mar-2026.

items.target: Buybacks activated whenever the discount to last-published NAV (adjusted for S&P/ASX 200 hedged-to-NZD moves) exceeds 6%
items.notes: Discount widened past this threshold through mid/late 2026 (reaching 11-13% by late July), and the Company has been an active buyer of its own shares under the programme (up to 5% of shares on issue in any 12-month period).

items.target: 1.25% of gross asset value p.a., reducible to a 0.75% floor for underperformance versus the NZ 90-Day Bank Bill Index (0.1% reduction per 1% of underperformance)
items.notes: For H1 FY2026, the gross return underperformed the Bank Bill Index by 7.4 percentage points, triggering the fee floor of 0.75%; a $607,768 management-fee credit note was accrued as at 31-Dec-2025 to offset future fees.

items.target: 10% (plus GST) of excess return above the Bank Bill Index + 7% hurdle, capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV, subject to a high-water mark
items.notes: No performance fee was earned or expensed in either H1 FY2026 or FY2025 (the Manager did not achieve a return in excess of the hurdle/high-water mark); FY2024 did see a $364k performance fee paid.

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Andy Coupe (Feb-2026): 'We acknowledge that it has been a tough period for the Barramundi portfolio' — several holdings substantially underperformed, with losses concentrated in information technology and classified-advertising positions amid AI-related investor concerns; management added BHP and Rio Tinto to capture commodity strength. Senior Portfolio Manager Robbie Urquhart expressed continued conviction in the fund's technology holdings, arguing they remain valuable to clients and are integrating AI capability effectively, i.e. framing the recent derating as a valuation reset rather than a change in underlying business quality. FY2025 commentary (Aug-2025) similarly described the year's return as 'disappointing' despite global market strength, attributing the shortfall to 'poor financial results from a handful of companies' the Board and Manager view as temporary in nature, while expressing confidence in the medium-to-long-term resilience of the portfolio and noting a positive start to July trading.

bull_case: The Barramundi discount to NAV has widened to 11-13% by mid/late 2026, well beyond the 6% share-buyback trigger — active, funded buybacks at this discount are directly NAV-accretive for remaining shareholders and a potential mean-reversion catalyst if the discount narrows back toward its historical single-digit range

PIE tax-efficient structure gives NZ investors simplified, favourably taxed exposure to a diversified basket of Australian growth/quality names (WiseTech, Xero, CSL, Macquarie, BHP) without direct ASX brokerage, FX conversion or FIF/FDR tax complexity

The manager fee reduction mechanism (1.25% down to a 0.75% floor during underperformance) partially self-corrects and aligns the Manager's economic incentives with a return to outperformance, unlike many fixed-fee LICs

8% p.a. headline distribution yield provides substantial current income for yield-focused investors, funded by a systematic quarterly payout policy that has been maintained since 2009 regardless of market conditions

This is fundamentally a value-of-underlying-assets-plus-discount-closing thesis, not a growth-compounder bet: a buyer today is effectively acquiring ~$1 of diversified, liquid, ASX-listed equities for roughly 85-90 cents, with the potential for both the discount to close and for underlying Australian equities (WiseTech, CSL, Xero, BHP, Macquarie) to recover from the AI-driven technology derating
bear_case: This is an income/NAV-discount vehicle, not a growth compounder — total shareholder return is capped by whatever the underlying Australian equity portfolio earns, minus a real and permanent fee drag (1.25% management fee plus potential 10% performance fee above a demanding hurdle), so buy-and-hold investors are structurally disadvantaged versus simply owning a low-cost ASX 200 index ETF unless the discount closes or the Manager consistently beats benchmark after fees, which it has recently failed to do (FY2025 +3.9% vs benchmark +13.5%; H1 FY2026 -6.6% vs benchmark +5.6%)

The 8% p.a. distribution policy is NOT organic income — the portfolio's actual dividend yield is closer to 2%, so in any year the adjusted NAV return falls short of 8% (which has been true recently), the quarterly payout is substantially a return of shareholders' own capital, mechanically shrinking the NAV per share over time even before considering fees

Persistent and recently widening share price discount to NAV (11-13% through mid/late 2026) shows the market structurally distrusts the vehicle's ability to convert NAV into shareholder value — buybacks help at the margin but have not been sufficient to prevent the discount from widening as performance has deteriorated

Recurring warrant issuance is a structural dilution risk: the Aug-2025 tranche (85.2m warrants, $0.70 strike, exercise date 7-Aug-2026) is now deeply out-of-the-money given NAV has fallen to ~$0.53-0.54, illustrating how warrant terms set against a prior, higher NAV can become a value transfer risk to shareholders in periods (like the one just experienced) of falling NAV, and a new dilutive tranche is likely to be issued again in due course per the recurring capital-management programme

Sub-scale size (market cap roughly NZ$150-230m and falling with NAV) limits secondary-market liquidity and the fund's relevance to larger investors, and provides no offsetting diversification benefit since the portfolio is 100% concentrated in a single country (Australia) and effectively a single asset class (ASX-listed equities) that a NZ investor could access more cheaply via a low-cost hedged ASX 200 ETF
